articles.title: Can social media bans protect young people’s mental health? Early research suggests that bans aren’t the answer
articles.author: Ari Lightman, Professor of Digital Media and Marketing, Carnegie Mellon University
articles.summary: Kids have found ways around most of the safeguards meant to keep them off social media platforms.
articles.contentHtml:
The year 2026 has been an expensive one for social media platforms.

Since March, YouTube and Meta, the parent company of Instagram and Facebook, have settled or paid out in multiple lawsuits to the tune of more than US$17 billion for allegedly acting negligently, deliberately designing their platforms to hook kids and misleading the public about safety and privacy. If these suits are any indication of how states and the public are starting to view social media platforms, more may follow.

On top of these lawsuits, social media platforms are facing a loss of business as bans for minors are accelerating and spreading worldwide. Australia was one of the first with a ban on kids under 16 on social media starting in December 2025, followed soon after by the U.K. with a similar prohibition.

The current list of countries looking to ban minors from these platforms tops more than 20, from Greece to the United Arab Emirates to Canada. The proposed and enacted bans around the world vary in terms of age restriction, parental consent rules and age verification methods. Different countries are looking at restricting different platforms, but most include a mix of Snapchat, YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, Facebook and X.

These bans aren’t necessarily for mental health reasons only – some are motivated by political concerns about foreign-owned platforms, and others aim to protect young people’s privacy. But nearly every government banning social media platforms for young people mentions their mental health as a reason.

The question is, are these bans the solution to the mental health problems young people are facing? I research digital media and marketing and measure the impact of new technologies, and I’m skeptical about whether prohibiting access to these platforms will actually improve young people’s mental health.

Mental health concerns

Since Jonathan Haidt’s 2024 book “The Anxious Generation” critics of social media have increasingly focused on young people’s mental health. Haidt argues that social media disrupts kids’ social and neurological development, contributing to rising anxiety and depression through sleep loss, fragmented attention, addiction, loneliness, social comparison and perfectionism.

A 2026 study found that young people between 14 and 20 are more than 100% more likely to experience mental illness than 14- to 20-year-olds 50 years ago.

Increased use of social media and screen time is compounding an already precarious time for minors. In 2021 it was estimated that 20.5% of young people experienced elevated symptoms of anxiety, and 25.2% of youth reported elevated symptoms of depression globally.

Many factors contribute to this, including better screening and awareness of kids’ mental health problems, as well as societal disruptions as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic. As the world sheltered in place and moved online for work, school and social interactions, there was an increase in isolation and loneliness.

Not all bad

In light of these concerns, some researchers argue that bans on social media platforms are like putting an age restriction on buying alcohol or cigarettes.

But unlike these addictive and potentially harmful substances, there are benefits to social media, especially for teens who feel disconnected from their local communities and want to build relationships with others who feel similarly.

Social media platforms allow for global connectivity and community-building with like-minded groups. They also provide a place for self-expression and civic engagement.

In a Pew survey of U.S. teens, 80% said social media helps them stay connected to what’s happening in their friends’ lives.

Show me the money

One place where the comparison with tobacco is actually quite apt is in relation to the money from lawsuit settlements.

In 1998, states settled a lawsuit against the major tobacco companies to recover smoking-related healthcare costs. Part of the settlement was allocated to programs aimed at reducing youth smoking. In 2026, total state funding for these programs amounts to just 3.4% of the $21.7 billion in revenue states will collect from tobacco settlement payments and tobacco taxes.

Similarly, some money from an August 2026 Meta settlement with a group of states for $17 billion is slated for state-based programs focusing on mental health infrastructure, school and community programs, and public health campaigns.

However, there is no oversight or direction as to how states should use the funds, nor is there a mechanism to report how that money has improved kids’ mental health care, safety and well-being.

Is it even possible?

Early evidence from the Australian social media ban shows that kids are finding work-arounds: Roughly 61% of kids ages 12–15 continue to access platforms using false IDs, altered appearances or virtual private networks, or VPNs, even though millions of accounts were disabled. In fact, this has become so common that U.K. lawmakers are debating restricting consumer VPN access.

Some countries, such as Australia, require the platforms themselves to develop ways of verifying a user’s age. Some minors have bypassed scans from biometric age estimation technology by using photo manipulation software, substituting celebrity photos, using clever makeup and even utilizing older friends and parents to pass the “selfie tests” on their behalf. Others simply manipulate their birth years during registration or rely on existing adult-verified accounts managed by family members.

And all of these age-verification methods, whether developed by a government or a social media platform, rely on collecting sensitive data to estimate age accurately, which creates privacy concerns.

Australia is currently seeking to raise fines on social media platforms that fail to comply with its requirements. The Australian safety commissioner, charged with enforcing the ban, issued a compliance update that showed 7 in 10 children who held accounts in restricted platforms remained on those platforms, and more than 80% of Australian teens ages 10-15 still use social media frequently.

Beyond concerns about enacting and enforcing these restrictions, some policymakers also worry that total bans could push some kids to migrate to even riskier online spaces.

What could work

Based on the evidence, I’m not convinced that banning social media platforms will be an effective solution to the mental health crisis among young people today.

So what could work?

Supporting young people’s mental health is a complex endeavor that will require a combination of people, organizations and resources coming together.

I believe kids’ mental health would be better served by governments enforcing safety by default standards on social media platforms rather than outright bans. This means that the highest security and privacy options are in place by default so that minors still on a platform are protected. For instance, accounts would be unsearchable by default, so users would have to intentionally make a profile change to be found by people they don’t know in real life.

Safety by default standards also place limits on the manipulation, algorithmic restraint and other addictive mechanisms that may lead to psychological harm in vulnerable populations such as young people.

Educating kids on digital literacy and online safety as well as ensuring some screen-free time are also going to help support kids’ mental health.

It’s also important for parents and other caregivers to recognize changes in behavior as a result of addiction to social platforms and screens. And when adults start seeing signs of a problem, they need clear, easy and affordable ways to connect their kids to mental health support, which is not available in most places right now.

And finally, the United Nations recommends bringing kids into the conversation about what’s best for them online. Obviously, this does not mean putting 12-year-olds in charge of regulatory agencies. But feedback from young people about what they care about, what they get out of being online and what makes it hard for them to look away from their screens could inform changes to social media platforms and education programs that could help young people engage online more safely and maintain a healthy balance.

Ari Lightman is affiliated with Jewish Healthcare Foundation

articles.title: Restraint can leave mental health patients traumatised. New research reveals what they need afterwards
articles.author: Nutmeg Hallett, Associate Professor of Mental Health Nursing, University of Birmingham
articles.summary: New research suggests that the support patients receive after being restrained can affect how safe they feel and whether they regain trust in their care.
articles.contentHtml:
Most of us know what it feels like to be ill and frightened. Now imagine being held down by the very people responsible for your care.

This can happen in mental health hospitals when staff believe someone poses a risk to themselves or others. Patients may be physically restrained, locked in a room alone or given medication to calm them quickly. These measures are known as restrictive interventions. Although they are intended to prevent harm, they can cause serious injuries and, in extreme cases, death.

Our research suggests that what happens after a restrictive intervention can affect how people recover from the experience. The support they receive may help them feel safe again, while a lack of support can add to their distress.

Concerns about the use of force in mental health care go back almost 200 years. In 1839, psychiatrist John Conolly introduced a policy at Hanwell Asylum in Middlesex that ended the use of mechanical restraints such as straitjackets and handcuffs. However, historical research shows that Conolly continued to advocate locking patients in rooms alone, a practice known as seclusion.

Today, restrictive interventions remain part of mental health care. Research has shown that these experiences can be deeply distressing and sometimes traumatic, even when staff consider them necessary to prevent harm.

Read more: Restraint in mental health hospitals: what families want staff to understand

Some patients experience nightmares, intrusive memories or symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) long after the intervention has ended. A review of patients’ experiences of mental health hospitals also found that fear of restraint could discourage people from seeking help.

Yet much less attention has been paid to what hospitals can do to support people afterwards.

A 2022 review of 21 studies found that patients frequently reported feeling frightened, powerless and unheard during restrictive interventions. Many also described poor communication from staff afterwards, leaving them with unanswered questions about what had happened. Some felt that once the immediate incident was over, it was forgotten by the staff involved. For the patient, however, the experience could remain distressing for months or even years.

We wanted to understand how mental health services could respond more effectively.

In our research, we examined 35 research publications and policies obtained from 46 NHS mental health trusts in England. We also worked with patients, carers and mental health staff to understand what people need following restrictive interventions.

Although NHS guidance recommends that patients receive support and have opportunities to discuss incidents, a separate analysis of hospital policies found considerable variation in how that support was described and organised.

Support needs to continue beyond the incident

One important finding was that talking about what happened can be valuable, but the timing and approach are crucial.

Immediately after being restrained, someone may still be frightened, angry or overwhelmed. They may need reassurance, practical help or simply some time and space before they feel ready to discuss the experience.

Being offered a conversation at that moment may feel like another demand rather than an opportunity for support.

But if a patient declines to talk immediately, they may receive no further opportunity. Our research suggests that declining a conversation should not mean losing access to support altogether.

Instead, support should continue, with opportunities to discuss what happened when the person feels ready.

When patients do want to talk, their needs may differ. Some want to describe how the experience affected them, while others want to understand why staff acted as they did. They may also want to explain what could have been handled differently.

Whatever the conversation involves, patients want to feel listened to, understood and taken seriously. Having some choice over when and where the conversation happens, and who takes part, can help restore a sense of control after an experience in which they may have felt powerless.

Our research also found that people wanted to know their concerns had made a difference. This could mean changes to their individual care plan or improvements in how the hospital responds to similar situations.

Without any visible response, conversations risk becoming a box-ticking exercise that leaves patients feeling dismissed.

Providing this kind of support also depends on the wider hospital environment. Staff need the time and support to listen to patients, reflect on what happened and act on what they learn.

A frightening experience cannot be undone. But being ignored or dismissed afterwards can deepen the harm, while compassionate support may help patients begin to rebuild their trust in the people caring for them.

The findings offer a lesson that extends beyond mental health hospitals. When someone has experienced something frightening, the way others respond afterwards can become an important part of their recovery.

Nutmeg Hallett receives funding from the National Institute for Health and Care Research. Nutmeg Hallett is a member of the Green Party.

John Baker receives funding from the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR). He is currently a NIHR Senior Investigator and Chair of the NIHR Doctoral Clinical and Practitioner Academic Fellowship (DCAF)

articles.title: We compared what happens after a schizophrenia diagnosis in Denmark and the UK
articles.author: Ricardo Twumasi, Lecturer in Psychosis Studies, King's College London
articles.summary: It turns out where you live matters. A lot.
articles.contentHtml:
Schizophrenia is one of the most severe mental illnesses. This makes it an important test of how well countries support those with the most complex needs.

Schizophrenia can involve hearing voices, delusions and difficulties with thinking, motivation and everyday activities. It does not mean having a split personality and improvement is possible.

But recovery is about more than just having fewer symptoms. It means a life of value: healthy relationships, a home, good physical health and something meaningful to do, which is often work or study.

Yet, research shows that in both Denmark and the UK, two countries with publicly funded healthcare systems, just under half of those with schizophrenia are in work, education or training early in their illness. But as life with schizophrenia progresses, that number drops to around one in ten.

Health Gap / Sundhedskløften is a collaborative series from The Conversation UK and Denmark’s Videnskab.dk exploring what the two countries can learn from each other when it comes to health and wellbeing.

From cycling and alcohol to inequality, healthcare and everyday habits, the series looks beyond hospitals and medical treatment to explore how culture, politics and society shape the way people live – and how healthy they are.

So what can both countries learn from each other when it comes to better care? What helps someone build a life after diagnosis – and how does that differ between Denmark and the UK?

From diagnosis to treatment

In both countries, people with a first episode of schizophrenia are usually referred to a specialist team. In England (where most of our UK examples come from), early intervention in psychosis teams serve people between 14 and 65, and support can be offered for up to three years.

Denmark’s equivalent, Opus, is mainly for 18- to 35-year-olds and support normally lasts for two years.

Both teams combine medication with talking therapy, involvement of family and help with study or work. With Opus, a named contact coordinates this care and links with the local council. Research has found that this approach reduces symptoms more than standard care.

The care someone with schizophrenia receives in the UK is much more of a postcode lottery compared with Denmark. England’s 2023-24 national audit of early intervention teams found that 93% of teams in the east of England met the “performing well” standard, compared with just 21% in the south west.

Research shows that the end of that specialist care is a fragile moment in both countries. Interviews with people coming to the end of their care with early intervention teams in England found that people valued the care they had received, but some felt abandoned when it ended. Interviews with people in Denmark with long-term mental illness described how hard it was to find their way through services.

In and out of hospital

When someone needs a hospital bed, the two countries struggle in different ways. In England, a shortage of beds means some people are sent far from home, sometimes hundreds of miles away. At the end of July 2026, there were 285 “inappropriate” out-of-area placements. This meant that a national goal to end the use of these out-of-area psychiatric placements by 2021 was missed.

In Denmark, the pressure shows mainly as crowded wards. In the Central Denmark Region, only one psychiatric department briefly dropped below its 90% occupancy target during 2024.

Leaving hospital also shows where services are well connected and where they are not. Similar to the UK, psychiatric hospitals in Denmark are run by one government department, while local councils run housing support, social care and job centres.

Denmark’s 2025 psychiatry plan found that patients who could not leave hospital without council support waited on average for 43 days in psychiatry, compared with just four days in physical healthcare.

England has the same split between NHS hospitals and councils – that are responsible for social care and housing – this presents similar problems. Indeed, people stuck on mental health wards waiting for supported housing cost the NHS in England £102 million between 2024 and 2025.

Work rarely offered

Both countries have employment specialists within mental health teams to help people find a job. In a Danish trial of 720 people, this kind of support was found to lead to more time in work or education than the usual job services.

Neither country offers this service consistently everywhere, although Denmark aims for every psychiatric service to work this way by 2028.

In our Danish study, we followed more than 65,000 people with schizophrenia for up to ten years after diagnosis and in terms of employment status, we found that work, training or education accounted for 48% of the weeks we recorded.

While an audit in England and Wales found that in community psychosis care only 2% of people looking for a job had been offered work. Treatment and support alone cannot remove that barrier.

Health checks and follow-up

Antipsychotic medicines can also have side-effects. These can include increases in weight and blood sugar levels. And poor physical health in schizophrenia is often overlooked.

In both countries, it’s mainly GPs who must spot and treat the diabetes and heart disease that can follow. In Denmark, research has found that people with schizophrenia and diabetes are often tested as much as others. But in England,fewer than three in five people living with severe mental illness had a full physical health check in the last year.

So while it’s clear that both countries already monitor the quality of care, the task in both places is to use that evidence to make support dependable.

This is important because success should be judged by whether people can build lives they value. Ideally, a diagnosis should be the start of a plan for living, not the end of one.

This series was commissioned as part of a partnership between Videnskab.dk and The Conversation, where articles are published in English and Danish.

Ricardo Twumasi has received funding from OpenAI, Deloitte LLC and Danmarks Nationalbank. Ricardo Twumasi is a visiting Forsker for Region Hovedstaden and holds an honorary contract with South London and Maudsley NHS Foundation Trust

Frederikke is Data Scientist at the Center for Clinical Research and Prevention. Frederikke Hørdam Gronemann has previously received funding from The Capital Region of Denmark Research Fund, The Independent Research Fund, and The Jascha Foundation.

Merete Osler receives funding from the Independent Research Fund Denmark and the Lundbeck foundation.

articles.title: Why adoptive families can struggle to get help until they reach crisis point
articles.author: Claire Agius, Lecturer/Researcher, Manchester Metropolitan University
articles.summary: Adoptive parents can spend years helping children feel safe after early trauma, often while struggling to find support for their own mental health.
articles.contentHtml:
In a deeply personal passage of his first Labour Party conference speech as UK prime minister, Andy Burnham paid tribute to the care workers who had looked after his father, Roy, who had Alzheimer’s disease and had died just two weeks earlier.

Those workers were “holding a threadbare system somehow together”, he said, yet remained “invisible to the political class of this country”. Addressing them directly, he added: “You are not invisible to me. I see you. I thank you.”

His words made me think about the care that goes unseen within families. Why are some forms of caring recognised as care, while others become almost invisible simply because they are considered part of family life?

I research trauma and adoption, and I am also an adoptive parent. I’m familiar with the story often told about adoption: a child finds a permanent family, a new life begins and everyone lives happily ever after.

But my research focuses on what happens after that supposed happy ending, particularly when the effects of a child’s earlier trauma continue into their adoptive family. And Burnham’s words made me wonder how much of the care provided by adoptive parents goes unrecognised simply because we call it parenting.

In England and Wales, an adoption order makes adopters the child’s legal parents. But a legal order cannot erase what happened beforehand.

Children adopted from care are often described as “previously looked-after”, a phrase I have long struggled with. There is nothing necessarily “previous” about the effects of their early experiences. A child may be physically safe but still struggle to feel safe. Earlier experiences can affect their development and their ability to trust the adults closest to them, since a family can be permanent in law long before a child feels secure enough to believe that permanence will last.

Adoptive parents are therefore living alongside the effects of experiences that happened before they even knew their child. This can make the parenting very different from what people usually imagine.

The relationship offering safety can also be the relationship in which fear and mistrust are expressed. For some families, this includes child-to-parent violence and abuse. A child experiencing overwhelming distress may run away or behave in ways that put themselves or others at risk. Parents may find themselves calling the police to protect their child or another family member, or because they fear for their own safety.

Understanding the reasons behind a child’s behaviour does not protect a parent from the emotional and physical impact of living with it. A parent can see why their child is hurting and still be hurt themselves.

My colleagues and I have researched compassion fatigue among adoptive parents raising children affected by early trauma. Compassion fatigue describes the emotional exhaustion and disconnection that can develop through repeated exposure to another person’s trauma.

My doctoral research also explored adoptive parents’ mental health more broadly. Parents described feeling exhausted while continuing to hold family life together. Sometimes, the very fact that they were managing made their distress harder for others to recognise.

The effects can reach beyond parents and children, affecting siblings and other family members. The adversity may belong to the child’s past, but its consequences can become part of the whole family’s present.

When families struggle to get help

Families are also affected by what happens outside the home. At school, a frightened child may be seen simply as badly behaved. A child who cannot get through the school gates may become an attendance problem. When the reasons behind their behaviour are overlooked, attention can quickly turn to what the parents are supposedly doing wrong.

Parents described fighting for help while feeling judged or blamed, sometimes until their family reached breaking point. Professionals, meanwhile, described recognising that families needed support but working within services that could not always provide it.

This is where Burnham’s description of a “threadbare system” particularly resonated with me. I have often described the services surrounding adoptive families as both traumatised and traumatising. Professionals are working under enormous pressure, often without the resources needed to respond to families’ complex needs. And when services are struggling, their responses can add to the distress of children and parents who are already finding life difficult.

For families, this can mean reaching a crisis and then having to demonstrate just how bad things have become before support is available.

Burnham’s words were powerful because they acknowledged care workers whose contribution is too often overlooked. But they also invite a wider conversation about what society recognises as care in the first place.

Care can come with a uniform and a job title. It can also mean a parent staying close to a child whose earliest relationships taught them that the adults they depend on may not always be safe or able to stay.

Helping a child learn to trust those relationships can take years, and the emotional demands on parents can be considerable. That work deserves recognition and support.

Care should not become less deserving of either simply because we call it parenting.

Claire Agius does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: France’s student uprising and young people’s mental health – what are the common causes?
articles.author: Maria Melchior, Epidémiologiste, Directeur de recherche, Inserm; Sorbonne Université
articles.summary: Two researchers explore the connections between France’s ongoing student movement and mental health related to academic pressure and conditions in secondary and higher education.
articles.contentHtml:
KEY TAKEAWAYS

  • Links between conditions in schools and higher education institutions in France and young people’s mental health are up for debate amid the student protest movement.

  • Studies objectify the psychological difficulties experienced by many young people, from middle school onwards, more frequent among girls than boys.

  • This data can be compared to results documenting their feelings about their schooling: pressure, impact of Parcoursup (the French national admissions platform for first-year higher education programs), overcrowded classrooms…

Since mid September 2026, tens of thousands of high schoolers and students have been taking action across France to demand better teaching conditions: more supply teachers, timetables that better suit their needs, well-maintained buildings and an overhaul of Parcoursup, the national higher education admissions program, pointing out social inequalities within the secondary education system and at university.

Their demands illustrate widely felt pressure at school and anxiety, attributed to a learning environment that is not conducive to psychological wellbeing. Can studies shed any light on the subject? What is the state of young people’s mental health in France and what are the links with conditions in schools?

Surveys on middle and high school students’s psychological difficulties

Since the 2000s Adolescent mental health has been determined by the HBSC (Health behavior in School-Aged Children) and ESPAD (European School Survey Project on Alcohol and Other Drugs) surveys along with France’s own national EnCLass survey, since 2018. Edition after edition, they have shown a high level of psychological difficulties.

Adolescence is, by definition, a period of emotional, physical and social transformation, and the fact that it is synonymous with psychological difficulties for some young people is common knowledge.

Nevertheless, the results of the population monitoring carried out in the Enclass survey show an adverse trend accelerated by the Covid-19 pandemic – if during lockdowns the entire population was twice as anxious and more depressed than before, adults returned to more usual symptom levels after the pandemic ended, which wasn’t the case for young people.

According to the latest EnClass data collected in 2024, 45% of middle school students (enrolled in 6th, 5th and 4th grades) reported experiencing at least one psychological complaint (depression, irritability or nervousness) more than once a week for at least 6 months, 32% reported feeling nervous, 29% irritable and 21% depressed.

These types of psychological difficulties are systematically higher among girls and increase with age. In boys, levels of psychological distress appear to be slightly lower compared to the 2022 EnClass survey.

Among high school students, the situation has considerably deteriorated: 19% of high school students are significantly prone to depression, 20% reported having had suicidal thoughts in the previous 12 months, with 15% having attempted suicide at some point in their lives.

In adults, depressive episodes and anxiety disorders are more frequent between 18-29

Psychological difficulties may persist after the end of schooling in secondary education. France’s Public Health Barometer – Santé publique France revealed that, in 2024, young people aged between 18-29 are the adult group most affected by episodes of severe depression – one in five (21%) were affected during the 12 months preceding the survey, nearly 7% reporting a severe episode of depression.

Similarly, generalised anxiety disorder is also more common among young people aged 18 to 29 than among other age groups: 8% are affected.

Finally, young people aged between 18-29 also emerge as the age range who report the most suicidal thoughts (8.6% in the 12 months preceding the study) and suicide attempts (6.7% had already attempted suicide in their lifetime). The latter result is surprising, given that suicide attempts are cumulative and rates are expected to increase with age.

It could indicate that young people, particularly affected by suicidal acts, remember it better than other groups. There could also be a generational effect, with young people born in the early 2000s more affected by suicidal tendencies than previous generations for multiple reasons – deteriorated mental health, an increase in poverty, the influence of content diffused on social networks – it can only be confirmed in the longer term.

Young people’s mental health has deteriorated since Covid-19

Data from Santé publique France on young people seeking medical help confirms a deterioration in young people’s mental health since the Covid-19 pandemic: in 2024, girls aged 11-17 and all 18-24-year-olds were groups being admitted to accident and emergency rooms for self-inflicted acts, including suicide attempts, with levels relatively stable since 2021.

The rate of hospitalisations for self-inflicted acts was higher in 2024 than in the previous three years, with particularly high levels among girls aged 11-17 and among young people aged 18-24 of both sexes.

Young people’s mental health during Covid-19 and socioeconomic inequalities

More than five years after the end of the Covid-19 pandemic, the level of mental health problems among adolescents and young adults in France is high, a trend also observed in other countries. The context of armed conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East, climate change and content circulating on networks certainly contribute to these levels of “unease”.

But the worsening of social inequalities could also play a role: in France, the poverty rate rose from 14% of the population in 2016 to 15.4% in 2024, which is the highest level in 30 years, and a high level that tallies with the European Union average. The group most affected by poverty – 30% of people – are single-parent families, in which about 25% of adolescents in France grow up.

Pressure, the classroom environment, baccalaureate reform… How are conditions in schools affecting students?

Alongside these societal and macroeconomic determinants, what role does the schooling environment play? France’s youth is regularly vocal about stress surrounding Parcoursup, the higher education admissions system that is based on results from the final two years of high school.

School pressure, against a backdrop of broader concerns about the academic and professional future, features among the stressors that can increase the risk of anxiety and depression symptoms in young people. Meanwhile, the international study Health Behavior in School-Aged Children (HBCS) conducted under the auspices of the World Health Organization in Europe (WHO), in Central Asia and Canada, shows that French students are not the ones who complain the most.

On the other hand, French students are among those who have experienced an unfavourable evolution in recent years, especially young girls. In 2014, 40% of 15-year-old girls in France reported they had experienced a high level of school-related pressure, while eight years later, 60% of them did.

The pressure can come from school curricula to cover and assessment methods. It can also reflect learning conditions and how much students are receiving the support they need from their teachers.

French teenagers are also distinguished by lower than average levels of trust in their teachers: 35% of 15-year-old students say their teachers support them, compared to 42% on average. At the same time, 48% of them, compared to an average of 53%, said they felt supported by their peers.

The Pisa Surveys (International Program for Monitoring Student Achievement) confirm these results, as has outlined the findings of the CNAM and the French Centre for Educational Systems Studies. In 2022, 18% of 15-year-old French students reported that teachers were not interested in each student’s achievement, compared to 11% on average. Half of French students additionally complained about noise and unrest in the classroom, and France features in the high end of countries where students tended to be less self-confident and more likely to report fear of failure.

These trends can be compared to the increase in class sizes in general and technological (vocational) high schools and colleges, from 27 per class in 1990 to more than 30 in 2023.

The impact of France’s baccalaureate reform in 2018 must also be taken into consideration, which, by removing certain fields of study, may have individualised educational pathways and split class groups by isolating students and making it more difficult for them to find support from their peers. This is a hypothesis that should be examined in future research in order to prove it right or wrong.

School pressure also comes from students’ perception of what comes next after high school. If, in 2024, nearly eight out of ten baccalaureate students continued their higher education studies, only about 35% of students who enrolled in undergraduate studies obtain a degree within three years, while 55% leave university without a degree, in comparison with 45 and 40%, the respective rates in the European Union.

Finally, if France invests, on average, around 15,000 US dollars per student (which is currently equivalent to about 13,500 euros) throughout their schooling and corresponds to about 5% of gross domestic product, and is comparable with the averages observed in OECD countries, investment in higher education remained stable between 2015 and 2022, while the number of students increased by 20% during the same period. This translates into a relative decline in the share of public funding for higher education, from 80% in 2015 to 75% in 2022.

This relative decline in the resources invested in secondary and higher education could result in the deterioration of learning conditions from a students’ point of view – teachers are not replaced, a decrease in the attractiveness of France’s exam process for becoming a certified teacher in France, resulting in the employment of poorly trained contract teachers, and problems affecting admissions for thousands of baccalaureate holders due to a lack of places in higher education.

Young people’s mental health is directly linked to the environments in which they grow up, both physical and virtual, and the school system that they are part of undeniably influences their individual experiences, their stress levels and the sense of injustice and concern that many of them express.

The reasons why high school students are taking action today may well be, at least in part, for the same reasons why their mental health has deteriorated in recent years.

A weekly e-mail in English featuring expertise from scholars and researchers. It provides an introduction to the diversity of research coming out of the continent and considers some of the key issues facing European countries. Get the newsletter!

articles.title: A crackdown on online shopping tricks is welcome, but doesn’t go far enough
articles.author: Nauman Wajid, Lecturer in Marketing, Birmingham City University
articles.summary: Consumers don’t need the extra pressure to purchase.
articles.contentHtml:
Hurry! Only two left! Fourteen people bought this in the last hour! Fifty people are looking at this item!

Anyone who shops online will be familiar with these kinds of messages popping up on their screen. The online equivalent of a pushy salesperson, they are designed to create a sense of urgency around making a purchase.

These online tools are sometimes referred to as “dark patterns” – clever tricks built into apps and websites to encourage you to do things you may not necessarily want to do – like click the “buy” button. One large study revealed that over 11,000 shopping websites use these strategies.

For years this was seen as an inevitable – and irritating – part of online shopping. That’s beginning to change. The UK’s main consumer regulator, the Competition and Markets Authority, has been probing retailers on these very issues for the past few years.

And there have been noticeable successes against companies using misleading countdown timers and urgency claims, which they have since agreed to stop.

The CMA also has sharper teeth than before. Since April 2025, it has been given direct enforcement powers, including the ability to impose fines of up to 10% of a business’s worldwide turnover.

And there are new rules due in early 2027 on subscription contracts that will tackle practices such as pressure selling at renewals and hard-to-cancel subscriptions.

This is all real and meaningful progress.

The CMA is trying to track down deception. Was the countdown clock real or not? Was the previous price quoted ever actually charged?

But there is another effect of dark patterns that regulation doesn’t yet touch – what happens to you psychologically, after weeks, months, or years following the experience of being treated as the victim of these tactics, whether they’re technically accurate or not.

Research shows that scarcity cues, such as countdown timers, not only affect purchase decisions, but they also create a sense of time urgency and increased mental load on customers .

Studies have suggested a kind of emotional exhaustion, known as “digital burnout” that can occur due to heavy usage of digital consumer platforms, which are constantly fed to individuals via the algorithms they have developed.

Even a compliant, accurate countdown timer is designed to generate a sense of urgency and panic. A true “only two left” still makes you feel pressured.

Pressure to purchase

My own ongoing research looks at the potential impact of AI-powered personalisation and nudging, which is getting more sophisticated every day. It is already becoming extremely adept at reading shoppers’ behaviour.

Read more: Drunk online shopping is big business – but who is responsible?

And this sort of pattern has been observed by researchers before. The psychological toll of constant algorithmic pressure is a distinct problem from whether or not a given claim is false.

The CMA can put an end to companies misinforming you on the matter of scarcity. It doesn’t have a way to correct for the effect over time of constant and accurate urgency messaging on stress levels or decision fatigue, which it’s not currently asked to address by the consumer protection law.

The question of whether something is true or not is one thing. But the effect that question has on consumers is an entirely separate issue that customers need to be aware of.

The CMA’s new powers give the regulator a credible deterrent that it did not have before. But they are yet to address the more complex and elements of dark patterns, which relate to how they actually make people feel.

Nauman Wajid does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Mental disorders are twice as common among victim-survivors of intimate partner violence
articles.author: Megan Willis, Associate Professor, School of Behavioural and Health Sciences, Australian Catholic University
articles.summary: Yet victim-survivors often don’t or can’t access mental health care.
articles.contentHtml:
Open a newspaper on any given day and you’re likely to read about yet another case of intimate partner violence – a form of domestic violence between current or former partners.

Less visible is what happens to the victims who survive it. For them, the mental health consequences can persist long after the relationship ends.

Our new research, published in the Journal of Family Violence, found mental disorders were twice as common among victim-survivors of intimate partner violence.

What we did

We analysed data from more than 7,000 Australians who had been in an intimate relationship, drawing on the nationally representative Australian Child Maltreatment Study.

Participants reported whether they had ever experienced three forms of intimate partner violence: physical, sexual and psychological violence (such as emotional or financial abuse).

Participants were also assessed for major depressive disorder, generalised anxiety disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and alcohol use disorder.

What we found

More than half (55.3%) of Australians who had experienced intimate partner violence met criteria for at least one of the four mental disorders, compared with 24.5% who had not.

Each of the four mental disorders was more common among people who had experienced intimate partner violence.

The prevalence of mental disorders was similar across those who had experienced psychological, physical or sexual violence, although many had experienced multiple types of violence.

These findings do not establish that intimate partner violence caused mental disorders. Participants reported whether they had ever experienced intimate partner violence, while the mental disorders identified were current or lifetime. This means we can’t determine which came first.

However, other studies have found that mental health problems often emerge after experiencing intimate partner violence.

This suggests at least some of the mental health burden is likely to be a result of the violence.

Read more: 1 in 3 men report using intimate partner violence. Here’s how we can better protect women – and help men

Adversity accumulates

Among victim-survivors, mental disorders were more common for those with a history of multiple types of child maltreatment. This included emotional, physical and sexual abuse, neglect and exposure to domestic violence.

Almost two-thirds (62.5%) of those with a history of multiple types of child maltreatment met criteria for a mental disorder, compared with 39.1% of those with no history of child maltreatment.

This suggests that a history of child maltreatment may leave people more vulnerable to mental disorders if they experience intimate partner violence later in life.

This adds to the many reasons why preventing child maltreatment is so important.

When child maltreatment does occur, early mental health support may help reduce the risk of mental disorders in adulthood.

Can people get the help they need?

Despite how common mental disorders are among victim-survivors, many don’t access appropriate care. Around two in five Australians who experience physical or sexual violence from a former partner don’t seek advice or support.

For those who do seek help, support is not always accessible. Specialist domestic and family violence services are struggling to meet demand.

People seeking mental health care through the broader health system can also face significant barriers, including cost.

Addressing these gaps requires investment in specialist domestic and family violence services, as well as affordable and accessible mental health care across the broader health system.

GPs, psychologists and other health professionals also play an important role in identifying and responding to intimate partner violence. This requires effective approaches to identification, appropriate training and clear pathways to specialist support.

Seeking help should feel safe

We also need to consider what happens to the information survivors share when they seek help. This is particularly relevant for those involved in legal proceedings, where confidential health records may be subpoenaed.

Family court proceedings are one example. More than 80% of parenting matters before the court involve allegations of family violence. During these proceedings, psychology, counselling and GP records can be subpoenaed and may be accessed by a former partner.

This can undermine the therapeutic relationship and discourage people from seeking or continuing therapy.

Practitioners have described broad subpoenas as “fishing expeditions” and raised concerns they may be used as a form of systems abuse.

Family law reforms introduced in 2025 strengthened protections for these records. But these protections are not automatic. Survivors may need legal assistance to know they exist and how to access them. It’s too early to know how effectively the reforms are working.

Seeking mental health care following intimate partner violence should not unnecessarily compromise a survivor’s privacy, particularly when there is no evidence their mental health affects their capacity to parent.

We need to prevent violence in the first place

Experiencing emotional and physical abuse in childhood, as well as witnessing domestic violence, is linked to an increased likelihood of experiencing – as well as perpetrating – intimate partner violence as an adult.

The benefits of preventing child maltreatment and reducing children’s exposure to domestic violence extend into their adult relationships.

Read more: Western Australia is experiencing a child safety crisis. Here’s what would help

There are also opportunities to intervene earlier once intimate partner violence begins.

In one Australian study, around one in three women experienced psychological abuse without physical or sexual violence. Among those who experienced multiple forms of violence, psychological abuse typically came first.

Early signs included isolation, controlling behaviour and verbal abuse. This can involve limiting a partner’s contact with family or friends, controlling aspects of their day-to-day life, or insulting them.

These behaviours may be difficult to recognise as abuse initially. Possessiveness, jealousy or attempts to limit contact with family and friends may be framed as signs of love or concern.

Helping people recognise these early signs may create more opportunities to intervene sooner. This means ensuring awareness campaigns depict what psychological abuse can look like early on.

The National Sexual Assault, Family and Domestic Violence Counselling Line – 1800 RESPECT (1800 737 732) – is available 24 hours a day, seven days a week for any Australian who has experienced, or is at risk of, family and domestic violence and/or sexual assault.

The Men’s Referral Service – 1300 766 491 – is a national counselling, information and referral service for men who have chosen to use violence and want to change.

Megan Willis is a member of the NSW ACT Domestic, Family & Sexual Violence Research Network. The ACMS study received research funding from the National Health and Medical Research Council, with additional funding and contributions provided by the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, Department of Social Services, the Australian Institute of Criminology.

articles.title: Study of 20,000 Nigerians explores the links between drug use, climate change and poverty
articles.author: Abdullahi Abdulwahab Yakubu, Lecturer, Department of Psychiatry, Ahmadu Bello University
articles.summary: A staggering 67.5% of respondents relied on maladaptive coping strategies.
articles.contentHtml:
For years, the world has understood climate change as an environmental problem – melting glaciers, rising seas, extreme weather. But what happens in people’s minds when their world becomes unstable? What do they do when the only life they’ve known – farming, herding, providing for their families – becomes impossible?

These questions drove our team of psychiatrists and public health researchers to conduct one of the largest studies of its kind in west Africa. We interviewed 20,000 adults across 40 communities in Kano, Kaduna and Katsina states, a region that sits in the semi-arid Sahel belt. Agriculture is a major source of employment and livelihood in an area that is among the most climate-vulnerable in Nigeria.

Read more: One in two Nigerians live in poverty: why relief programmes have failed

We applied a number of research measures. We used a multidimensional poverty index to measure deprivation, the Kessler psychological distress scale to assess anxiety and depression, and the alcohol, smoking and substance involvement screening test to identify harmful substance use. We also asked participants about their coping strategies: how they deal with stress.

What we found is alarming. A vast majority of the people we surveyed are multidimensionally poor. Nearly half reported high levels of psychological distress. And almost one in five were engaged in substance abuse.

Our findings underscore that substance use disorder in north-west Nigeria can’t be understood in isolation. It’s part of a system – climate stress, poverty, mental distress – and must be addressed as such. The solutions exist: integrated mental health care, livelihood support, community-based interventions.

The research

The numbers tell a troubling story. A multidimensional poverty index measures not only income, but also access to education, healthcare and basic living standards. Over 85% of the people we surveyed were living in profound deprivation. This is significantly higher than the national multidimensional poverty incidence of 62.9% and reflects how extremely precarious this region is economically.

Using the Kessler scale, we asked about symptoms of anxiety and depression over the past month. Of our respondents 45.2% scored in the high range. To put this in perspective, studies in general healthcare settings in Nigeria typically find that 20% to 30% of people experience common mental disorders. Our figure suggests that climate-stressed communities represent a particularly vulnerable group.

Substance use screening revealed that 18.5% of our sample were engaged in high-risk substance use. Cannabis was the most common substance, used by 12.4% of participants, followed by prescription opioids like the painkiller tramadol (9.1%) and alcohol (7.8%). The widespread use of prescription drugs obtained without prescriptions is especially worrying because of the risks of dependence and overdose.

We also asked people how they coped with stress, using the coping strategies inventory. A staggering 67.5% of respondents relied primarily on unhealthy coping strategies; avoidance, emotional discharge, and behaviours that provide temporary relief but create longer-term problems. Substance use is a prime example of this pattern.

Behind the statistics are human stories of struggle and survival. In our interviews, participants spoke candidly about the pressures they faced and how they tried to manage them.

One farmer in his 40s told us:

When the farm fails, there is no money for food, let alone school fees. The worry does not leave my head. I take the local gin just to sleep at night.

A young man in his 20s described the temptation that surrounded him:

My friends use tramadol. They say it helps them forget that there is no work and no future. I have tried it too when the stress becomes too much. Everyone is doing something to escape.

A woman whose husband had left to find work in the city explained:

The men drink because they cannot provide. The women cry because there is nothing to give the children. This life is hard, and hard lives make people do hard things.

These voices remind us that substance use in these communities isn’t about pleasure or recreation. It’s about survival – a desperate attempt to numb pain that seems to have no other remedy.

What must be done

This isn’t just a health problem. It’s a development problem, an agricultural problem, a climate adaptation problem all rolled into one. The issues are interconnected and need to be tackled together.

There is a common misconception that substance use in poor communities is a moral failing or just a matter of personal choice. Our research suggests otherwise. It is often a direct response to overwhelming stress and hopelessness.

We identified three key responses needed:

  • Mental health and substance use prevention must be integrated into climate adaptation and food security programmes. If programmes are helping farmers to adapt to changing rainfall patterns, they should also be addressing the psychological distress they experience. If food aid is being provided, there should be screening for substance abuse at the same time, to help with early detection and possible intervention. Without this, we risk giving with one hand while the other hand loses the benefit.

  • Social protection schemes and livelihood diversification are essential. When people have other ways to earn income beyond rain-fed agriculture, they’re less vulnerable to climate shocks. This reduces the stress that drives substance use.

  • Civic and government interventions need to train community health workers to identify and refer people with mental health and substance use issues. There are too few psychiatrists in Nigeria to meet the need.

We found strong connections between poverty, psychological distress and substance use. People who are poor are more likely to be distressed. People who are distressed are more likely to use substances. These patterns are clear and statistically robust.

Why this matters

Our study was a snapshot taken at one point in time. Think of it like taking a photograph of a crowd; you can see who’s standing together, but you can’t tell who arrived first or who led whom. In the same way, while we can see that poverty and substance use go hand in hand, we can’t say which causes which, or whether both are caused by something else entirely.

Read more: Fighting climate change in the Sahel is worsening conflicts - new research shows how

Our evidence strongly suggests that climate stress leads to poverty, which leads to distress, which leads to substance use. But to prove that chain of events conclusively, we would need to follow the same people over several years, watching their circumstances change and their behaviour change in response.

This matters for aid providers because humanitarian and development programmes that ignore substance abuse are failing to address a key driver of poverty. When people use drugs or alcohol to cope, they become less able to work productively, less able to care for their families, and less able to recover from the next climate shock. Their health deteriorates, they face stigma, and they become trapped in a downward spiral.

Abdullahi Abdulwahab Yakubu does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Cannabis hospitalisations up 49% in a decade, new study shows
articles.author: Myfanwy Graham, NHMRC Postgraduate Scholar and Fulbright Alumna in Public Health Policy, Monash University
articles.summary: More people are ending up in hospital after using cannabis than a decade ago, and psychosis rates are rising. Here’s what can explain the rise.
articles.contentHtml:
Doctors have raised growing concerns about rising rates of cannabis-related psychosis.

Our new ten-year study shows those concerns are well founded.

We looked at almost 40,000 cannabis-related hospital admissions in Victoria between 2013 and 2023. Over that time, cases where cannabis was the main reason someone ended up in hospital increased by 49%.

Psychotic disorder (commonly called psychosis) was the leading cause.

What we did and what we found

We examined hospital records for 39,565 cannabis-related hospital admissions in Victoria over the ten-year period.

Admissions peaked during the COVID pandemic in 2020 and 2021. Cannabis-related psychosis was the main driver across the decade, accounting for 40.1% of hospitalisations where cannabis was the main reason. Poisoning made up less than 12% of cases.

These weren’t quick visits. Most patients (68%) stayed in hospital for longer than 24 hours, with the average stay lasting a week for all cases involving cannabis. This suggests these cases were serious. More than 1,500 people required admission to an intensive care unit (ICU).

Males aged 15–24 still represent the largest total group hospitalised. But our study showed the largest increase over the decade was in younger women and adults aged 65 and older.

Read more: Cannabis isn’t ‘safer’ in your 20s and 30s – it’s linked to an earlier onset of psychosis

What can explain the findings?

During 2020 and 2021, isolation, job losses and broader mental health struggles may have contributed to many people using more cannabis.

Wastewater monitoring confirmed a rise in cannabis use around this time. Unlike some illicit supply chains disrupted by border closures, local cannabis supply remained largely accessible.

Demographics in cannabis use are shifting too. The proportion of people who have ever used cannabis has risen over the decade. More women are also using cannabis in high-risk ways, including frequent use, which may increase the risk of cannabis dependence.

Changing social perceptions may play a role. As cannabis becomes more acceptable, people may simply feel more comfortable telling doctors about their cannabis use.

Higher-strength cannabis is also likely to play role. We are seeing severe psychiatric and respiratory reactions with products containing higher levels of tetrahydrocannabinol (or THC). That’s the component that can cause drowsiness or a high.

Is medicinal cannabis to blame?

It is hard to know if prescribed medicinal cannabis or illicit cannabis explains this increase in hospitalisations. Hospital coding systems – used in health records and in the data we examined – rarely distinguish between legal (prescribed) and illicit cannabis use; many people use both.

Fewer Australians take prescribed compared to illicit cannabis. Even then, legal products come with risks.

Higher-potency products that can be inhaled are generally not recommended for safety reasons. But these are some of the most frequently prescribed products, with some containing up to 88% THC.

High-volume telehealth clinics that don’t properly screen people for existing mental health conditions or other risk factors before prescribing high-strength cannabis may also be contributing to the rise in severe mental health adverse events.

Without proper clinical monitoring, risks may not be detected, or will be detected later, and harms may be more severe by the time problems are identified.

Read more: Medicinal cannabis has gone mainstream. But Australia’s struggling to cope

There are wider issues

This isn’t just a Victorian issue. In fact, some studies suggest other states have higher rates of cannabis use.

Nationally, cannabis remains one of the top illicit drugs leading to a hospital admission, outpacing illicit opioids.

International data shows a similar trend. When legal access expands via profit-driven commercial models, cannabis-related psychosis hospitalisations tend to rise.

Our findings that the largest increase in cannabis-related hospitalisations was in younger women and older adults has wider implications.

Public health initiatives don’t necessarily focus on these groups. By identifying who is most vulnerable, we have an opportunity to tailor prevention campaigns, improve clinical screening before cannabis is prescribed and more broadly for vulnerable groups, and ensure safety regulations keep pace with changing products and increased availability.

Myfanwy Graham receives funding from the Australian National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC). She has received state government and Department of Health, Disability and Ageing funding for independent reviews on medicinal cannabis. She has served as a consultant for the UNODC, WHO and NASEM, and is an appointed member of the Therapeutic Goods Administration's Medicinal Cannabis Expert Working Group. This article does not represent the views of the TGA or the Expert Working Group.

Suzanne Nielsen receives funding from the competitive research schemes (NHMRC, MMRF) and philanthropy. She is the current president of the Australasian Professional Society on Alcohol and other Drugs (APSAD). She has previously completed independent evidence reviews on medicinal cannabis for the TGA and Worksafe.

articles.title: ‘Lazy, weak, bewitched’ – how stigma stops Uganda’s children from getting help, and what schools can do about it
articles.author: Lydia Namatende-Sakwa, Associate Research Scientist, African Population and Health Research Center
articles.summary: School mental health programmes must address both emotional wellbeing and structural pressures such as poverty, stigma and exclusion.
articles.contentHtml:
“Me who is a poor person, do I have the luxury to have depression? No, it is only you who is rich that has the luxury to have depression.”

This statement, shared by a research participant in Kampala, the Ugandan capital, captures a persistent misconception: that depression belongs to wealthy people or those whose lives are comfortable enough to permit emotional vulnerability.

It is an example of how socio-cultural beliefs can become a barrier to recognising mental health problems and seeking support.

In 2025, Uganda’s Ministry of Education and Sports issued a set of mental health and psychosocial support policy guidelines and resources for schools. These included a training manual, teachers’ handbook and wellbeing guide. They provide practical information on recognising distress, psychosocial support, referral and wellbeing in education settings.

The next challenge is to put the guidelines into practice.

Our team of researchers at the African Health and Population Research Center did a study to provide evidence that would help schools in Uganda follow the guidelines. We looked at what people understand by mental health, what learners and staff need, school capacity and what needs to happen first to put the guidelines into action.

The study engaged 200 learners, teachers, parents, community representatives, policy actors and development partners across four districts: Kampala, Jinja, Gulu and Mbarara. Kampala is the capital city; Jinja is a mixed rural-urban context. Gulu is an area affected by conflict and displacement. Mbarara is an education and economic hub with urban and rural schools.

We found socio-cultural and gender norms strongly influenced whose distress was recognised, how it was explained and whether seeking help was considered acceptable. Mental health at school was linked to issues like literacy, spirituality, poverty, family instability, displacement, disability and trauma.

Learner distress reflected overlapping academic, family, economic, social and institutional pressures. The responses at school must take all these into account. School mental health programmes must address both emotional wellbeing and structural pressures such as poverty, stigma and exclusion.

Listening to Ugandans

Our four study sites were chosen to reflect a range of environments, with different resources and socio-cultural influences.

We held dialogues at each site with learners aged 13-18, parents, teachers, government representatives, youth-led organisations, religious and community leaders, NGOs and researchers. Special interest groups (including refugees, LGBTQ organisations and people with disabilities) were also included.

The dialogues explored understandings of mental health, learner and staff needs, school capacity and future priorities.

What’s influencing mental health

The study participants described student mental health as a growing concern. They mentioned depression, anxiety, stress, low self-esteem, fear, social withdrawal, substance use, bullying-related distress, trauma, anger, academic pressure and poor emotional regulation.

Participants described these as interconnected problems.

The drivers of distress among students were identified as:

  • academic pressure

  • family and home background, including absent parents, domestic violence and neglect

  • poverty that resulted in lower self-esteem and greater exclusion from peer groups

  • bullying, teasing, humiliation and harsh discipline

  • substance use and addiction, especially among boys and urban learners.

Boys and girls were seen as vulnerable to different pressures.

Barriers to getting help

Participants in all sites said mental illness carried a stigma. It was seen as morally wrong, caused by supernatural forces, or “a disease for the rich”.

Another perception was that boys and men couldn’t seek help for fear of looking weak.

Learners also felt they could not trust adults with their problems. They feared that teachers might judge them or reveal their personal stories publicly. Learners experiencing anxiety or distress thought they might be labelled lazy or badly behaved, or accused of “faking it” or “seeking attention”.

The danger is that withdrawal, poor concentration, anger or declining performance might then be treated as deliberate disobedience.

Mental health difficulties were sometimes attributed to witchcraft, curses or demonic possession. Religious and cultural systems can offer hope, belonging and support, but problems arise when they become the only explanation for distress. As one Kampala teacher warned,

Some people will pray until somebody dies.

Learners reported being told, “You have to be strong … a guy who does not cry.” Such expectations encourage boys to hide stress and may lead to withdrawal, anger or risky behaviour rather than seeking support.

Girls face pressures linked to harassment, poverty, reproductive-health stigma and social judgment, often while being expected to remain silent. Female educators also face gendered scrutiny, including questions such as, “Where are their husbands and why are they not interested in staying with them?”

Counselling can itself carry stigma. People reported fear and shame associated with getting professional help.

Changing systems to change norms

Teachers should recognise that a child’s behaviour may arise from bullying, poverty, bereavement or family conflict. Schools should ask not only “What is wrong?” but also “What may have happened?”

School mental health programmes should respect cultural beliefs without delaying appropriate help.

Girls should be protected from harassment and enabled to report problems confidentially. Schools should promote a broader understanding of masculinity in which recognising emotions and seeking help are seen as responsible behaviours.

Schools need private support spaces, clear confidentiality procedures and counselling that is normalised. Learners must be able to seek help before problems escalate.

Socio-cultural and gender norms are reinforced through everyday practices and cannot be changed through awareness messages alone. Uganda’s response must combine norm change with system change. Schools need culturally grounded mental health literacy, safe environments, respectful discipline, confidential support, gender-transformative programming, trained staff and links to health and community services.

The key question is whether schools can recognise distress without judgment and respond with dignity, protection and appropriate care.

Lydia Namatende-Sakwa does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Students from military families are often misunderstood in US public schools – a retired military officer and behavioral health expert explains what schools can do
articles.author: Nikki R Wooten, Associate Professor of Social Work, University of South Carolina
articles.summary: Students from military families have specific experiences and needs that require support from their schools.
articles.contentHtml:
Over 1.4 million children had a parent or caregiver who served in the U.S. armed forces in 2024.

Among active-duty families, 2.4% of military children had both parents serving in the military. Another 4% lived in single-parent households.

More than 90% of these children attend U.S. public schools. Over 67,000 attend Department of Defense schools located in the U.S. and foreign countries. Military-connected students have a unique set of experiences and academic and emotional needs, including support with school transitions and developing a sense of belonging at their new school.

Because only 6% of Americans have served in the U.S. military, some educators may not understand the experiences of military children and the challenges of military life.

As a retired U.S. Army lieutenant colonel and military behavioral health expert, I think there are a few key ways that school districts can better support these students through school transitions.

Some strategies include identifying military-connected students during enrollment and training educators about military life.

Benefits and drawbacks of military life

The military lifestyle creates both unique opportunities and challenges for children and teenagers whose parents are military service members.

Military children often travel and have opportunities to live in multiple cities across the U.S. and other countries. They are also exposed to different cultures, new traditions and opportunities to learn foreign languages.

These children are resilient and adaptable. They may also display increased independence, personal growth and pride because of their parent’s military service. Many are thriving in school because of these traits.

Military children are also twice as likely to serve in the military as their civilian peers.

But military life can also be stressful for children.

Many children with parents in the military move frequently. They often live in more cities and attend more schools than their civilian peers – an average of two schools during high school, and for most, six to nine different schools between kindergarten and 12th grade.

They experience their parent being away from home for various periods of time, ranging from a few weeks at a time to a year or more.

They also fear that their parent might be hurt or killed while serving in the military.

As a result, military children and teenagers may experience social withdrawal, angry outbursts and mental health problems, including depression and anxiety. These challenges might also cause them to miss school, struggle to complete school assignments and have difficulty making new friends.

Recent research found that military-connected students were more likely to be disengaged in school and repeat a grade than their civilian peers. Other studies found that multiple parental deployments and longer parental separations affected children negatively. Examples include greater family stress and behavioral problems.

A stressful experience

Children’s responses to military life vary, depending on how old they are and their level of maturity. Children 5 and younger often have limited language skills to express their feelings. As a result, they may act out behaviorally in response to changes in caregivers and daily routines.

Elementary school students may have tantrums, be clingy, have toileting accidents, engage in uncontrollable crying or become less talkative as a result of changes in schools, homes and caregivers.

Middle school students and preteens, ages 8 to 13, are likely aware of how their lives are different from their civilian peers.

These students may have experienced multiple moves and attended multiple schools over their relatively short lives. They may respond to changes in schools and household routines with angry outbursts, irritability, anxiety and social withdrawal.

They may also have fluctuating grades, peer conflict, problems completing their homework and disciplinary problems at school.

Boys and girls may express their stress differently. Boys may exhibit more anger and aggression, whereas girls might demonstrate sadness, depression and self-harm.

Military adolescents and high school students, typically 14-18, have heightened risk for anxiety, depression and suicide due to military-related stressors, especially during parental deployments.

They may experience mood changes, anger and social withdrawal. They may also disengage from school activities, perform poorly in school and choose to skip classes. Many are also high achievers despite the challenges of military life.

Military adolescents are also at risk for substance use.

My prior research from 2019 found that military adolescents had frequent emergency department visits and hospitalizations for substance use problems during the Afghanistan and Iraq wars.

How schools can support military-connected students

Military-connected students transitioning to a new school often need help early in the process to ensure they have adjusted well to their new school.

As a licensed clinical social worker and former child therapist for military children, I think brief check-ins with a school counselor or social worker are necessary to identify concerns early. These check-ins can help avoid behavioral or academic difficulties and prevent a problem from becoming worse.

U.S. public schools are required to identify students with an active duty military parent, typically by asking about military affiliation during enrollment.

Some school districts also include children of veterans and those with parents in the National Guard and Reserves in these records.

Research has consistently shown that the impact of military life continues after parents leave military service.

An estimated 2.3 million children under 18 reside with a veteran who is disabled. These children often assume caregiving responsibilities for siblings and their veteran parent.

Identifying schools that support military-connected students

State education departments can give schools a Purple Star School designation, indicating that the school is committed to assisting with the academic, social and emotional needs of military-connected students. These schools maintain a list of military students, help students with school transitions and train school personnel about the challenges of military life.

Currently, there are over 4,100 Purple Star Schools in 44 states across the U.S.

The proportion of military-connected students in U.S. public schools depends on the military and veteran population of each state and school district, as well as the geographical location of military installations.

Texas, California, Florida, North Carolina, Georgia, South Carolina and Virginia rank among the 10 states with the most military families that have children attending public schools.

Schools can help military-connected children and their families by creating a welcoming school climate, maintaining open communication with students and parents, and developing student groups and peer-support programs.

Frequent school guidance counselor, nurse or social worker visits may also be needed. High schools can develop peer-mentoring programs and suicide prevention, mental health awareness and anti-stigma campaigns.

I think it is also important for schools not to rush to identify behaviors as a disciplinary problem when family stress is the root cause.

Although military-connected students face unique challenges to success in school, I think schools should intervene early and often to meet their needs. Helping these students ensures every child has an equal chance to succeed in school.

Army after over 33 years of military service.
